chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: Diksha's trip to Delhi starts the chapter, and you try blocks before you learn any name. Then each new idea comes as a short story, and a tool lets you try it. Your maths book's questions are answered on the tool. A short look back ends the chapter.

points.title: Try first, then name it
points.text: You pick blocks for a building before anyone names a solid. The names come after you have tried.

points.title: A story, then a tool
points.text: Each new idea is a short story with a problem. The tool next to it lets you test the idea yourself.

points.title: The same three steps in every tool
points.text: Get ready with a picture from the story. Play and try things. Then answer your maths book's questions on the same screen.

points.title: One look for every solid
points.text: Every prism is blue and every pyramid is magenta. A cube is teal and a cuboid is red. A sphere is coral, a cone is yellow and a cylinder is orchid. Real things, such as a die or a brick, keep their own look.

points.title: Real things around you
points.text: Pictures show real buildings, dice, gates, rugs and wheels. Every answer the plan makes starts with From the picture or Sample answer.

points.title: Help is always there
points.text: Every tool has a Hint, a Reset and Back and Next buttons. Squiggly and Wiggly bring the web and matchstick puzzles.

tool_config.learning_objective: Students pick solid shapes for the roof, pillars and base of a building and compare the model with the real building.
tool_config.screen: Frame as in every tool: progress dots on top, Back and Next at the sides, a Hint button. Book questions come one at a time, each in a small panel with its answer choices, such as cards, numbers or Yes and No. Every answer the tool shows starts with From the picture or Sample answer. PHASE 1, get ready: Diksha's mat from the story. Her wooden blocks lie in front of the India Gate drawing. One line says, Help Diksha build a model. Nothing is scored. PHASE 2, play: three buildings sit on top: India Gate, the sandy-brown gateway with tall minarets and the round thatched hut. Pick one. Drag blocks from the tray to a base pad, pillar pads and a roof pad. Every block in the tray can be used again and again. A block that cannot rest where it is put rolls or slides away, so you see which blocks stand firm. Tap Compare to put your model beside the real building. No block has a shape name written on it. PHASE 3, the six questions of your maths book: build the model, tap the parts you used (roof, pillars, base), pick why you chose them, pick a block for each part, then pick what is alike and what is different when the model sits beside the picture.

5. An acute angle is less than a right angle. An obtuse angle is more.
6. Look again at the straw shapes. A triangle is rigid. A four-sided frame with joints is not.
7. Look again at the folding gate. Its slanted diamond cells squash when it moves.
8. Shapes with three or four sides can have a different number of right angles.
9. Look again at the round paper. A circle has a centre. A radius goes from the centre to the border.
10. A diameter goes through the centre. It is double the radius.
11. A flat shape can be sorted by its sides. A straight-sided shape has as many angles as sides.

Students recall right, acute and obtuse angles, the parts of a circle and how to solve the shape puzzles.

objectives.objective_text: Students say what all bricks have in common and pick shapes to stack for a model of a tall tower.
Students say that solids can be sorted by the shapes of their faces into prisms and pyramids.
Students name the face shape that all prisms share and the face shape that all pyramids share, and say if a cube is a prism.
Students name and count the faces, edges and corners of a solid.
Students count the parts of straw and clay solids, work out F+V−E for each and sort solids by flat faces and straight edges.
Students say that two faces of a die can be opposite each other or can meet at an edge.
Students find the face opposite a given face and the faces that share an edge with it, on a die and a coloured cube.
Students spot rectangular, triangular and curved faces on everyday objects.
Students mark everyday objects that have a rectangular, triangular or curved face, or no corner.
Students say why a solid that fits two rules belongs in the part where two circles overlap.
Students sort solids into two circles by a rule and place a solid that fits both rules in the overlap.
Students say that a tower of cubes is built in layers and that some of its cubes are hidden from view.
Students build cube models, count the cubes in a tower including the hidden ones and complete cube drawings on triangular dot paper.
Students use the numbers of faces, edges and corners of a solid to say which solid it is.
Students pick or build the solid that fits clues about its faces, edges and corners, or about its straws and clay balls.
Students explain that a net is a solid opened out flat and that it folds back into the solid.
Students match nets to solids, test which nets fold into a given solid and find the solid from the pieces of its net.
Students say that two lines meeting at a point make an angle and find angles in everyday pictures.
Students make an angle by meeting two straws at a point, then mark and count the angles in pictures.
Students make a right angle by folding paper twice and use it to find right angles in objects and drawings.
Students test the corners of shapes and objects with a paper right angle and draw right angles on a dot grid.
Students compare an angle with a right angle and say whether it is acute, right or obtuse.
Students swing a line against a right angle to tell acute angles from obtuse angles, then draw and mark both kinds.
Students say that a shape which keeps its shape when one side is pushed is called rigid.
Students push one side of a straw triangle and a straw rectangle and say which one keeps its shape.
Students notice that the four-sided shapes of a folding gate lean over when it is pushed.
Students push a rectangle, a square and a pentagon and say how their angles change.
Students count the right angles in three- and four-sided shapes drawn on a dot grid.
Students draw three- and four-sided shapes on a dot grid, count their right angles and tell shapes apart by their kinds of angles.
Students name the centre of a circle and the radius, a line from the centre to the border.
Students form a circle from equal straws and from points marked at the same distance from a centre.
Students say that a crease that folds a circle in half is called a diameter.
Students show that the folds of a circle are equal diameters through the centre and that a diameter is double the radius.
Students point out the centre, radius and diameter of a round carpet design and of wheels.
Students draw a circle design, mark its centre, radius and diameter and compare wheels by radius and diameter.
Students sort flat shapes by the number of their sides and count the angles of each.
Students sort flat shapes by their sides and by their angles and find that a straight-sided shape has as many angles as sides.
Students find shapes hidden in a drawing and say how lines cut a shape into smaller shapes.
Students find the hidden shapes in a drawing and draw lines that divide a shape into smaller shapes.
Students count the shapes in a web, big and small, and say what a walk that uses no wall twice means.
Students count the triangles and rectangles in two webs and decide which walks can be made without using a wall twice.
Students count the triangles made from matchsticks and say how moving or taking away sticks changes the count.
Students make, move and remove matchsticks to form a given number of triangles.
Students recall the faces of prisms and pyramids, the parts of a solid and which nets fold into solids.
Students recall right, acute and obtuse angles, the parts of a circle and how to solve the shape puzzles.

visual_key.wooden_blocks: light brown wooden blocks: cuboids of different sizes, a cylinder, a cube and two half-round blocks, lying on a floor mat in front of a drawing of India Gate (real wood: the blocks keep the light brown of wood, as in the book, and are not in the solid colours)
visual_key.india_gate_drawing: a drawing of the India Gate arch in sandy brown on a white sheet that stands up behind Diksha
visual_key.other_buildings: two small buildings drawn beside the first task: a sandy-brown gateway with tall minarets and arches, and a round hut with a thatched straw-coloured roof and pale walls (the book does not name them)
visual_key.street_model: a small model street on a green base: a grey road, small houses with red, orange and blue roofs, two round brown huts, a lamp post
visual_key.qutub_minar: a tall tapering reddish-brown tower with balconies that narrow towards the top, shown with a few bushes at its foot
visual_key.qutub_model: a small stepped stack of three green boxes, each smaller than the one below (real boxes in a real picture, so they keep their own green; the book shows a boy holding it; in the image it stands on a table, with no child)
visual_key.bricks: three solid blocks side by side: a red-brown clay brick, a grey stone block and a brown wooden block (three real materials, so they keep their own colours), all true cuboids with flat faces and square corners, shown from one angle so three faces of each can be seen
visual_key.diksha: a girl with a ponytail, a yellow top and a pink skirt (as the book draws her)
visual_key.nitesh: a boy with dark hair and a light blue t-shirt, cutting a net out of paper with orange scissors
visual_key.squiggly_and_wiggly: two black fuzzy spiders with large round eyes and a thin hanging thread; Squiggly makes the triangular web, her brother Wiggly the web of rectangles
visual_key.box_net: a pink paper box opened out flat with dotted fold lines, which folds back into the box (a real paper box, kept pink as in the book)
visual_key.paper_strip_ball: a ball made of curved orange paper strips joined at the top and bottom, with a small green leaf on top (a paper craft, kept orange as in the book; it is not the sphere of the solids)
visual_key.prisms: shaded 3D solids, ALL in the one prism blue (as the book draws them), with dashed hidden edges: a triangular prism, a square prism and a hexagonal prism; every other prism of the chapter (the triangular prism of the sorts, a pentagonal prism if one is ever drawn) is this same blue
visual_key.pyramids: shaded 3D solids, ALL in the one pyramid magenta (as the book draws them), with dashed hidden edges: a triangular pyramid, a square pyramid and a pentagonal pyramid; every other pyramid of the chapter is this same magenta
visual_key.straws_and_clay: thin straws joined at their ends by small round clay balls to make a skeleton of a shape; every straw is its own straight line and every ball its own dot, drawn see-through so no edge hides another and all can be counted: straws are the edges and balls the corners (cube and cuboid 12 and 8, triangular pyramid 6 and 4, square pyramid 8 and 5, triangular prism 9 and 6). In a SOLID skeleton the straws are in the colour of the solid they make (cube teal, cuboid red, every prism blue, every pyramid magenta) and every clay ball is one plain clay colour (a warm grey-brown); in a FLAT straw shape (the triangle, rectangle, square and pentagon of the push tools) the straws stay green, yellow, blue or orange as in the book and the balls red or pink, because a flat shape is not one of the solids
visual_key.die: a standard grey-white die (a real die, so it keeps its own colour, not the teal of the maths cube) with dots in the usual patterns; opposite faces always add up to 7 (1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4), so two faces that add up to 7 are never in view together; the book's picture shows 5 on top, 1 in front and 3 on the right (it writes numerals, the plan draws the same faces with dots, the same on the image and on the tool)
visual_key.colour_cube: one cube with six differently coloured faces (red, orange, green, purple, dark blue, yellow), shown in three views side by side; the six face colours are the question's own data, so this cube is NOT teal; the three views are drawn as in the book and must all fit one single cube with one colouring
visual_key.border_objects: about twenty pencil sketches of everyday objects around a page, in plain pencil outline with no colour so the child's red, blue, smiley and star marks show: dice, erasers, balls and a football, cans and bottles, an ice-cream cone, a party hat, TWO CHEESE PIECES, a Rubik's cube, a gift box, a wooden wedge, a cake slice, a pyramid made of small triangles and a double pyramid; in the plan each is drawn as the book draws it: the ice-cream cone is a plain cone with no scoop, every ball is a shaded ball, a can is a cylinder, the wooden wedge and the cake slice are triangular prisms, and each cheese piece is a PYRAMID: a point at the top, two triangle faces in view with a few small holes, a flat base, as in the book; a cheese piece is never drawn as a wedge or a prism
visual_key.sorting_circles: round outlines in dark purple-blue on a pale green panel with green italic labels; one panel has two separate circles, another has two circles that overlap
visual_key.cube_models: four models of unit cubes, A, B, C and D, drawn in the shapes of the book (D is a stepped model of layers, a wide base layer with a smaller layer above each and one cube on top); every unit cube is a shaded teal cube, as every cube of the chapter, so the four models differ in shape only (in the book they are red, purple, yellow and blue, teal, pink and green); every unit cube drawn with its own edges so the cubes can be counted
visual_key.cube_towers: two stacks of unit cubes, every cube a shaded teal cube (light teal tops, teal left faces, green-teal right faces, as the book's second tower is drawn): a stepped tower of 4 layers (4 by 4, 3 by 3, 2 by 2 and 1 cube: 30 cubes), the layers told apart by their steps and not by colour, and a large plus-shaped tower: a middle column of 6 cubes and four stairs going out from it, each stair with columns of 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 cubes (6 + 4 × 15 = 66 cubes); the plan draws every cube with clear edges so the layers and columns can be counted
visual_key.triangular_dot_paper: grey dots in a slanting triangular grid (evenly spaced rows, each row shifted half a step, so any three neighbouring dots make an equal triangle) with one finished cube outline in teal (the cube colour) and two cubes drawn only in dotted lines that run exactly through dots
visual_key.sphere: a proper shaded 3D ball with a soft highlight, round from every side, always in the one sphere colour, a coral red (a lighter tint of red than the cuboid's deep red, so a sphere and a cuboid on one screen are never alike); never a flat disc
visual_key.solid_pictures: shaded 3D pictures, each a true solid, each in the colour of its solid: a coral-red sphere, a magenta square pyramid, a yellow cone, a red cuboid, a pink-purple cylinder, a teal cube and a small blue triangular prism lying on a rectangle face with its two triangle ends clear (the book's small orange solid, read as a triangular prism); and a second set in the same colours: a coral-red sphere, a yellow cone, a magenta triangular pyramid, a teal cube and a red cuboid; every sphere is a shaded ball, a cone has one round flat base and one point, a cylinder has two round flat faces and a curved side
visual_key.nets_and_solids: line drawings of nets with dotted fold lines (violet in one question, dark green in another; a net is flat and is NEVER in the colour of the solid it folds into, so the colour cannot give the match away) with a solid beside or below each, drawn in the colour of its solid (cylinder pink-purple, cube teal, cuboid red, prisms blue, pyramids magenta); the pieces of Nitesh's net are pale orange (one pentagon and five triangles); every face of a net is its own flat shape joined to the next along a dotted fold line, so the faces can be counted; the nets of the book's question 4 are drawn as printed (A and C do not fold)
visual_key.angle_mark: a small red arc at the corner of an angle, or a small red square for a right angle
visual_key.straws_angle: two straws, one green and one orange, meeting at one end to show an angle, with a red arc or red square at the corner
visual_key.yoga_figures: five simple yoga figures with round heads in blue and orange, each with a red arc where two limbs meet
visual_key.house_and_boat: a blue house with a darker blue roof and a boat with a brown hull and a cream sail on a thick brown mast, with red angle marks at the corners
visual_key.right_angle_checker: a piece of pale orange paper folded twice so the folded corner is a right angle, marked with a red square
visual_key.dot_grid: rows of black dots on a white page, or on a pale blue, yellow, peach or pink rounded panel
visual_key.stick_figures: four simple stick people with round faces, whose arms and legs meet at angles
visual_key.rigid_shapes: straw shapes joined by red or pink clay balls: a triangle, a rectangle, a square of four equal straws (both lean over when pushed) and a pentagon of five equal blue straws; each clay ball is a joint that lets the shape turn, so a push tilts a four-sided or five-sided shape but never a triangle
visual_key.four_sided_shapes: three flat 4-sided shapes: a green shape with a slanted side, a pink slanting shape and an orange diamond
visual_key.equal_straws_circle: many straws in different colours, all the same length, laid like spokes round a central clay ball so their ends make a circle; and the same straws with unequal lengths, whose ends do not make a circle
visual_key.circle_paper: a round sheet of orange-brown paper with dashed fold lines through the middle (creases); a red circle for the radius and diameter picture
visual_key.compass_design: a yellow circle, then overlapping dotted circles, then a six-petal flower made of overlapping circles coloured blue, green, red and yellow
visual_key.carpet_design: a brown carpet with a fringe, a paisley border and an orange circle in the middle holding green and yellow petals around a small blue centre
visual_key.wheels: four wheels labelled A to D: a grey car wheel with four oval holes, a large brown wooden spoked wheel, a bicycle wheel with blue spokes and a thin black tyre, and a small dark tyre with a silver rim; each seen straight on so it is a true circle with its centre showing, in the printed sizes (B the largest, then C, then A, and D the smallest)
visual_key.hidden_shapes: red outlines drawn over one another: a circle, a cylinder, one square, one tilted rectangle (about 2.2 times as long as wide) and two triangles; the book has ONE square and ONE tilted rectangle here, not two squares. All the outlines are one red on purpose, so they hide one another; the cylinder here is a line drawing in that red, not a picture of the pink-purple solid
visual_key.dissection_shapes: flat coloured shapes: an orange long hexagon, a green square and a pink triangle on the left, and the smaller pieces they are cut into on the right
visual_key.shape_cards: six flat cut-out cards from the end of the book: an orange square, a green oval, a brown quarter circle, a light-green semicircle, a blue triangle and a pink circle
visual_key.spider_webs: purple threads on white: Squiggly's web is a long shape with 12 walls numbered 1 to 12 in dark red and point A at the bottom; Wiggly's web is a set of rectangles with a short bar at the top, point A at its upper right end and point B at the bottom of the middle-left line
visual_key.matchsticks: a thin wooden stick with a red-orange head at one end; all sticks the same length; shown singly, and in the two figures of the book, with every stick drawn whole so the sticks can be counted: Q3 is 9 sticks as three small triangles in a row, each touching the next at a base corner (the book draws small gaps there; the plan draws the corners touching, because only then can the puzzle be solved); Q4 is 13 sticks: a big triangle of side 2 made of 4 small triangles (9 sticks), plus one small triangle joined on its upper left side and one on its lower right side (2 more sticks each); all corners meet on one triangular grid
visual_key.angle_shapes: flat coloured 2D shapes: a blue square, a red triangle, a green slanting 4-sided shape, a purple right triangle, a purple pentagon, a thin green triangle and a red rectangle
visual_key.everyday_objects: four to eight familiar real objects, each a clean solid shape and none of them from the border sketches: for example a matchbox, a round tin, a marble and a toy tent, standing apart on a plain shelf in even light with nothing printed on them (real objects in a real picture: they keep their own colours). The tool's own shelf shows other things: a toothpaste box, a candle and a chocolate box shaped like a triangular prism
visual_key.toy_cube_tower: a small tower of identical plain toy cubes with no letters or pictures, stacked in layers on a table so the layers show; not the book's two towers; every cube the same size, teal like every cube of the chapter, with clear edges; each cube is a shaded 3D cube (a light top, a mid-teal front face, a darker side face and a soft shadow on the table), never a flat shape
visual_key.folding_gate: a steel folding gate across a doorway: slim straight steel strips of equal length crossing in a diamond lattice, pinned at every crossing and at the ends, shown half closed so every four-sided cell is a slanted diamond with two smaller corners and two bigger corners (a real gate's cells squash like this, they are not parallelograms)
visual_key.round_rug_and_wheel: a plain round woven rug and one bicycle wheel hung flat on a hook on a plain wall, each seen straight on so each is a true circle; not the book's carpet and not its wheels A to D
visual_key.plate_and_coin: a plain round steel plate and a coin lying apart, each seen straight on so each is a true circle (real objects in a real picture: they keep their own colours); not the rug, the wheel, the carpet or wheels A to D
visual_key.compass: a school compass: two arms joined at the top, a sharp metal point on one arm and a pencil on the other; the point stays fixed on the centre and the pencil draws the circle
visual_key.ruler_and_thread: a plain school ruler with equal tick marks and no unit written on it, and a loose thread, used only to compare lengths
visual_key.classroom_scene: a simple classroom: a desk and bench, a blackboard, a door, a window, a wall clock, and a book and a ruler on the desk; every corner drawn true so right, acute and obtuse angles can be found
visual_key.angle_pictures: five plain pictures: an open pair of scissors, a clothes hanger, a hand making a V sign, a seesaw and a slide; in each the two arms that meet are drawn clearly
visual_key.angle_letters: the capital letters V, A and Z in large plain strokes
visual_key.right_angle_figures: six flat coloured figures in a row: a blue rectangle, a green slanted four-sided shape, a purple triangle, an orange four-sided shape wider at the top, a purple slanted diamond and a red tilted rectangle (a little longer than wide, as the book draws it: it is a rectangle, not a square); every corner drawn true
visual_key.shape_gallery: fourteen flat coloured shapes numbered 1 to 14 in three rows, mostly four-sided (squares, rectangles and slanted shapes) with one dart-shaped number 1; every corner drawn true so right, acute and obtuse angles can be told apart
visual_key.isha: a girl of Diksha's age in simple clothes, drawn in the book's style; the book shows only her hands and straws, so the plan gives her one plain look and keeps it the same in every video
visual_key.dikshas_father: Diksha's father: a grown man in simple clothes, drawn in the book's style; the book names him in words only, so the plan gives him one plain look and keeps it the same in every video
visual_key.delhi_monuments: the real places named in the opener, drawn as they truly look with no invented building: India Gate, Qutub Minar, Safdarjung Tomb, Akshardham, the National Museum, Jantar Mantar and Sansad Bhawan

story.thread: Diksha visits Delhi with her father, sees its old and new monuments and tries to build a model of India Gate from her wooden blocks; the children and the spiders Squiggly and Wiggly then meet solid shapes, nets, angles, circles and shape puzzles.
story.setting: a floor mat where Diksha builds with wooden blocks after her summer trip to Delhi (India Gate, Qutub Minar and other monuments); a classroom and craft table with straws, clay, paper, matchsticks and a compass; two spider webs
